statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether police or drug detection ('sniffer') dogs at outdoor music festivals change whether people use, carry, buy or supply drugs there: the one study read measured what people said they would do in written scenarios, not what they did (Hughes et al., 2017). In a national online survey in late 2015 of 2,115 Australians aged 18 or over who had been to an outdoor music festival in the past year (mean age 22; recruited mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media; 89 in 100 had ever used an illicit drug and 78 in 100 recently), each person was assigned at random, by block, to two scenarios for a festival of 30,000 people; by the paper's paired analysis, one with no police and one of four policing scenarios: high-visibility policing (over 200 police), riot policing (over 400, including riot squads and mounted police), three sniffer dogs at the gates, or police working with health services. With any police, 72.8 in 100 said they would commit some drug offence, against 77.4 in 100 with no police; 69.6 against 76.5 said they would use drugs and 52.6 against 62.8 that they would carry drugs into the grounds, while 39.5 against 36.8 said they would buy drugs inside the grounds; stated giving and selling fell slightly (26.9 against 28.9; 3.5 against 5.1). With sniffer dogs, 66.3 in 100 said they would use drugs and 47.1 that they would carry them in; with police working with health services, 75.1 and 59.4, close to no police. About two in three said they would use drugs under every policing scenario, close to the 65.3 in 100 who said they had used drugs at their last festival. The strategies did not differ significantly in stated buying (43.8 in 100 with dogs; p = 0.711), so the paper's statement that dogs led to the most buying is not supported by its own test. The paper set significance at 0.001 but treats larger p values as significant, prints test results for giving and selling that differ between its text and table, and reports regression results whose outcome does not match its percentages (by the editors' calculation, the odds of not offending under high-visibility against collaborative policing are about 1.36, not the printed 2.69), so only the percentages are used here. The order of the two scenarios is not reported; the sample chose to take part, so the figures describe it, not festival-goers in general; and drug types and amounts were collected but not analysed, so the study says nothing about how much people would take, or about the hurried taking of drugs to avoid detection, a concern the paper cites from other sources. The authors suggest that buying inside the grounds could raise the risk of taking adulterated or mislabelled drugs, which the survey did not measure. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Do police and sniffer dogs at festivals stop people taking drugs? Not by much, going by what people said, and nobody measured what they actually did. In an Australian online survey, 2,115 festival-goers, most of whom had used drugs, read made-up festival scenarios with and without police. With no police, 77 in 100 said they would use drugs; with sniffer dogs, 66 in 100 still said they would, and with police working alongside health services, 75 in 100. Fewer said they would carry drugs in when dogs were there (47 against 63 in 100), but slightly more said they would buy drugs inside the festival when any police were there (40 against 37 in 100); the authors worry those drugs may not be what they are sold as, which the survey did not check. These are intentions in imagined situations, from people who chose to answer, and some of the paper's statistics don't add up. The survey did not ask how much people would take.
population: 2,115 people aged 18 or over living in Australia who had been to at least one outdoor music festival and one licensed entertainment precinct in the past year, recruited online in late 2015 mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media (mean age 22.3; 54.9% men; 89.1% lifetime and 78.4% recent illicit drug use; 47.0% ever stopped by police); 506 to 561 per randomized block
exposure: Written scenarios of policing at a 30,000-person outdoor festival: high-visibility policing (over 200 uniformed and plain-clothes police inside and outside), riot policing (over 400 police including public order and riot squads and mounted police), three drug detection dogs at the gates, or collaborative policing (police working with health organisations, first-aid tents and volunteers)
comparator: A written scenario with no police present, answered by the same people (order not reported); between strategies, the randomized blocks
outcome: Stated intention (yes or no) to use illicit drugs, carry them into the grounds, buy them inside, give them to a friend inside or sell them inside; perceived likelihood of detection. Actual behaviour was not measured
magnitude: Stated intentions, % (Table 4). Any police against no police: any offence 72.8 against 77.4 (−4.6 points; McNemar χ²(1) = 61.172, p < 0.001); use 69.6 against 76.5 (−6.9; χ²(1) = 102.063, p < 0.001); carry in 52.6 against 62.8 (−10.2; χ²(1) = 157.228, p < 0.001); buy inside 39.5 against 36.8 (+2.7; p = 0.001 in the text, < 0.001 in the table); give 26.9 against 28.9; sell 3.5 against 5.1 (p values differ between text and table). By strategy (high-visibility, riot, dogs, collaborative): use 67.9, 69.2, 66.3, 75.1 (p < 0.001); carry 51.7, 52.0, 47.1, 59.4 (p < 0.001); buy 38.3, 37.9, 43.8, 38.2 (p = 0.711); any offence 70.6, 72.7, 71.2, 76.6 (p = 0.003, above the paper's own 0.001 threshold). Detection judged likely or very likely for use or possession: dogs 52.3%, riot 32.9%, high-visibility 26.5%, collaborative 14.9%, no police 1.8%. Last festival (self-report): 65.3% used illicit drugs, 22.5% sold or gave drugs, 71.2% saw police. Regression odds ratios not used: editors' calculation from Table 4, odds of not offending under high-visibility against collaborative policing = (29.4/70.6)/(23.4/76.6) = 1.36 (of offending 0.73), against the printed 2.687.

evidence.locator: Methodology, 1st–3rd and 5th paragraphs (p. 93); Table 1 (p. 93); Methodology › Sample and recruitment (p. 94); Methodology › Data analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 94)
evidence.extracted: Purpose-built national online survey (late 2015) with five written festival scenarios built from 114 Australian police media releases and news articles (2002–2014) and focus-group tested: high-visibility policing, riot policing, drug detection dogs, collaborative policing and no police (police said to have left before the band the respondent wants to see). Each participant was block-randomised to receive two scenarios and asked under each whether they would use, possess (carry into the grounds), buy inside, give or sell illicit drugs; those saying yes were asked which drugs and what quantity. 2,115 eligible respondents (of 2,137 asked about festivals), recruited mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media; 506 to 561 per block. Any police (pooled) against no police compared with McNemar's matched-pairs tests; strategies compared by logistic regression; significance set at 0.001.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_hughes_2017 (RoB 2): high, for the outcome (stated intentions about hypothetical scenarios, answered by people who had just answered a contrasting scenario) and for selective reporting (no registration, half the survey reported, the stated significance threshold not applied, regression outcome inconsistent with the percentages, p values differing between text and table). A self-selected online sample recruited partly through drug forums.

indirectness.note: The claim concerns what people do at festivals; the study measured what they said they would do in written scenarios, in one Australian online sample in 2015, and collected but did not analyse amounts or drug types.

imprecision.note: 2,115 people; the differences in stated intentions are measured precisely, but they are not the outcome the claim is about.

grade.reasoning: Starts low: the main comparison, police against no police, is within person, with the order of the two scenarios not reported, so it is rated as observational; the outcome is a survey answer. Risk of bias −1 and indirectness −1 go below the floor: very low. The comparison between strategies was randomized between blocks, but would also be very low for the claim as worded (high, then risk of bias −1 and indirectness −2 for hypothetical intentions standing in for behaviour). Worded as insufficient evidence because no behaviour was measured; the percentages are reported as stated intentions of this sample, and the regression results and the paper's statement that dogs led to the most buying are not adopted. Status single study: the same team's 2014 pilot, described in the paper, was not read.
